analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal limits on lead in drinking water and forces utilities to test honestly, report publicly, and replace lead pipes fully.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in October 2017 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal drinking water rules to crack down on lead. Utilities would have had to report every lead test publicly, stop using sampling methods that hide lead, investigate the source of any lead finding, post online maps of where lead pipes are, and fully replace lead service lines instead of partially replacing them. It also would have cut the legal limit for lead in drinking water to 10 parts per billion by 2020 and 5 parts per billion by 2026 — far tighter than the 15 parts per billion trigger then in effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Families — especially children and pregnant women — whose homes are served by lead pipes or lead plumbing fixtures, and residents of older cities like Flint, Newark, and Chicago with large lead service line inventories. The bill gives them honest test results, fast notice when lead is found, maps showing where lead lines are, and a hard cap on the legal lead level.

how_it_helps.text: Requires water systems to report all lead and copper test results publicly, including the highest and most contaminated samples, and forbids sampling tricks that minimize the lead detected.
Requires on-site investigations of the source of lead within 10 business days whenever a test exceeds the action level, and direct notification to affected residents within 2 days.
Requires every water system to publish an online map of where lead service lines are, and bans the practice of 'partial' line replacement, which can temporarily make lead levels worse.
Caps the legal lead level in drinking water at 10 parts per billion by the end of 2020 and 5 parts per billion by the end of 2026, far below the 15 parts per billion trigger then in effect.

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities, which would bear the cost of more frequent and honest testing, on-site lead investigations, building pipe inventories and maps, and full replacement of lead service lines instead of the cheaper partial replacements then allowed. Those costs could flow partly into water rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not appropriate federal money, so the burden of mandated testing, investigations, inventories, and full service line replacement would fall on water systems and, ultimately, ratepayers — including in poorer communities where lead lines are most common.
Requiring on-site investigations for every sample above the action level and full testing of every tap in every school is a heavy compliance demand on small water systems with limited staff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and hard to dispute: better testing, honest measurement, faster notice when lead is found, and a lower legal limit for a toxin with no safe level, especially for children. The costs fall on water utilities, which would face more frequent testing, on-site investigations after any exceedance, public inventory maps, and more full pipe replacements; some of those costs would likely reach water customers' bills. Given that current rules allowed utilities to avoid detection in places like Flint and Newark, the design is reasonable — particularly the ban on partial replacements, which studies showed can briefly worsen lead levels. The one-year rulemaking deadline was ambitious but not unreasonable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee action, vote, or floor consideration ever followed before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on October 24, 2017, in the aftermath of the Flint water crisis.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, the only action the bill ever received.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still sitting in committee — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water utilities are better off, having avoided new testing, disclosure, and full lead-line replacement requirements; residents drinking from lead lines continue to bear the risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water utilities; lead risk stayed with residents

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill tightening lead drinking water rules in October 2017.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: 115th Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: The bill was never brought to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never advanced far enough for a roll call, so no vote record shows where either party stood.

industries.note: The bill would impose detailed sampling, reporting, inventory, and replacement duties on water systems, with more exposure when lead is found. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to ratepayers.

industries.industry: Water infrastructure and pipe replacement contractors
industries.note: Banning partial replacements and mandating full lead service line replacement would increase demand for full-line replacement work.
